description.source: Which of the following will be your primary campaign message?
What points do you wish to touch upon as you accept the Republican nomination? A written transcript will be transmitted to voters across the country.
You have the support of the important newspapers, and they are willing to accept your guidance on the proper campaign message. What do you want them to print?
What is your opinion on measures that would aim to restrict the sale or production of alcohol?
Some of the border states (Virginia, Maryland, Kentucky) are very close this year. Do you have a strategy to make these states jump to the Republican side?
The West Coast is a very competitive region. Can you make the case for Republican policies there, particularly in those places such as San Francisco which rely on foreign trade?
What is your definitive position on the tariff issue?
Can you state your definitive position on the American monetary system?
Will you send campaigners to Nebraska, in an attempt to deliver an embarrassing defeat to Bryan, or should those resources be focused on South Dakota, Wyoming, and Iowa?
Bryan's nomination has electrified the western voter, and he is now planning to campaign on the rails, six days a week. Will you break precedent as well and make a speaking tour of the nation?
The United States is in the midst of a financial calamity, with masses of unemployed men on the streets. What will you do to revive business in this country?
Grover Cleveland sent federal troops to Illinois to end the Pullman Strike without the request of Governor Altgeld. Was this an overreach on his part?
Some people have suggested implementing a minimum wage, under which people may not be employed. Do you think this would help increase wages or would it simply put more men out of work?
Do you have any comments to make about the candidacy of John Palmer, a Gold Democrat and splinter candidate who is currently campaigning?

You have received checks for $250,000 from J.P. Morgan and from Standard Oil, not to mention innumerable contributions from other concerned businessmen. How will you exploit this immense advantage in funding that you have?
Are you prepared to reaffirm our commitment to the Monroe Doctrine, should any new territories in Latin America gain independence from Spain?
Do you believe that the federal government has any right to issue interest-bearing bonds, such as those sold to J.P. Morgan in 1895?
Do you think that local jurisdictions should be allowed to use hanging or other forms of capital punishment for crimes?

Was it an appropriate intervention of the federal government to attach U.S. mail cars to Pullman trains during the strike in 1894? (Thereby making it a federal crime to interfere with the passage of these cars)

It has been alleged that opportunistic young women have married Union Army veterans for the sole purpose of exploiting the pension system. Do you consider this to be a form of corruption? Would you implement some standards that widows must meet before they can inherit these pensions?
Should Confederate veterans be included in the federal Civil War pension system?
Should there be greater regulation or even price controls on railroad shipping rates?
Will you work towards international agreements to create a monetary system based on "bimetallism", i.e. a combination of gold and silver?
Do you believe that immigrant labor is undermining the American worker? Should there be some restrictions put into place on immigration?
There is one week left until election day. Every state is important, but where will you give an extra push with what is left of your financial resources to educate the American voters?
I am a proud "wet" in the alcohol debate. What a man drinks is no one's business but his own.
It's a shame that Grover Cleveland allowed his supporters to bolt the party the moment it became clear their faction had lost this year's nomination.
Good riddance. On the issue of silver coinage, you are either with us or you're with the industrialists. Palmer has shown his cards.
I don't know how this man could live with four years of William McKinley just to save the face of his friend Grover Cleveland. No true Democrat would vote for him.
I'm very concerned about John Palmer. If he is gaining support maybe it means there is a valid criticism we must face up to.
My opponent's ideas are almost as dangerous to the survival of the United States as the Democratic traitors were in the 1860s.
I am the candidate who brings the reasonable, tested ideas of sound money, protection, and prosperity. Bryan on the other hand will usher in radicalism and instability.
My campaign will reach out to workers across the American spectrum, while Bryan's policies will leave them defenseless against foreign competition and will debase their wages.

My administration will bring back the era of the budget surplus, and will work towards the professionalization of the federal government. We will continue to phase out the 'spoils system' in accordance with the Pendleton Act.
I appreciate the faith of the American people and consult always with the Lord before I make my decisions. I will run a moderate, sensible agenda that appeals to the broad majority.
Labor agitators and agrarian radicals are threatening to overthrow our system of government. They have put forward a preposterous array of Constitutional Amendments and confiscatory welfare programs.
Democrats who believe in the gold standard are welcome in our party. We will increase tariffs, to be sure, but in a moderate way that addresses their concerns.
William Jennings Bryan makes an eloquent appeal to the heart. It's important for voters to realize that his solutions will not help our country.
Bryan's naked ambition knows no bounds. It is unbecoming of a candidate to make campaign appearances on his own behalf.

There's no way I can compete with Bryan's oratorical talents. Instead, I will receive groups of visitors at my home in Canton, Ohio. We have the financing to pay for these visits, and anyone who shows up will receive a free sandwich while I deliver a speech.
I will return these checks. It is not appropriate for politics to be infused with this kind of money.

We will print and mail campaign material in massive quantities. We will hire speakers to blanket the four corners of the nation. We will print ads every day in every major paper. Bryan cannot compete with us on money.
I can't attack Bryan like the papers can without losing some of my luster. Let them publish the defamatory cartoons and opinion pieces.

The big newspapers should remind the voters that I represent a return to prosperity after the Democratic disaster of the previous four years. They should be paying as little attention to Bryan as possible.
I'm not comfortable coordinating my message with the press. I trust that they will find the right way to present a contrast between me and my opponent.
Bryan would drive the important railroads of this region, such as Union Pacific, into bankruptcy by reneging on agreed-upon financing arrangements.
Bryan is the type of do-gooder politician who would attempt to impose his own morality on this independent region.
One of my highest priorities in office will be a canal through Nicaragua, which will greatly enhance our national trade. Democrats lack the ambition for such far-reaching projects.
Much of California's livelihood comes from gold mining. I reject any call to undermine gold through the free coinage of silver.
There is a certain element of conservatism in the southern states. I don't think that their temperament aligns with that of Bryan. I will simply repeat the message that he is a radical.
As a Civil War veteran, I am uniquely positioned to preach a message of sectional unity and Americanism. These states must know that we have allowed bygones to be bygones.
There is a burgeoning textile industry in the Upper South. Their success depends on cheap cotton, protection, and an absence of destabilizing labor issues.
I will remind them that we support Cuban independence.
We are running a 45-state strategy. I want our victory and repudiation of the silver Democrats to be as large as possible.
That's not a good idea. Let's be realistic and devote our efforts to the states that matter.
Our speakers should converge on Illinois from all directions. We need to blanket this state with advertising and with political parades.
Let's take the fight to Bryan. I want us to be campaigning the hardest in Missouri, Nebraska, Kansas, and Iowa. Our extra cash will ensure a landslide on election night.
Let's continue to focus on the Midwest. Ohio, Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, etc.
I want us to put all of our spare resources into Iowa and Minnesota.
We need to shore up our base. Let's make sure we win in Pennsylvania and New York, where the stakes are highest.
I support a strict adherence to the gold standard, which is fundamental to American prosperity.
Limited silver coinage is a good compromise. I support a program like that of Bland-Allison where the government purchases around $2 million of silver each month.

I support the free, unlimited coinage of silver at the current market price of 30-to-1 against gold. This ratio should be frequently adjusted to match actual prices in order to avoid another run on the Treasury's gold supply.
I support the free, unlimited coinage of silver at a fixed price ratio of 16-to-1 against gold.
Tariffs should be limited to the minimum amount necessary to raise sufficient revenue for the federal government.
In limited areas where we have new industries forming, tariffs can be higher. They should be low on most products.
Where we have mature, stable industries, tariffs can be lower. They should be high on most products.
We need high tariffs on a variety of products and commodities to stimulate American manufacturing.

The Democratic idea has been that if you legislate to make the masses prosperous, their prosperity will find its way up through every class which rests upon them. We need to help our farmers and our workers by allowing the coinage of silver.
It's time we think about implementing a series of public works projects to occupy our excess labor force. This will improve business by placing more money in the hands of consumers.
I can't stress this enough. The most important thing we can do right now is increase our tariffs to protect American business.
We need to reaffirm our commitment to non-intervention in business affairs. Companies need stability before they will have the confidence to expand.
This was the act of a tyrant. Pullman was engaged in abominable business practices, and in the darkest hour Cleveland cast his lot with the company over the working man.

Governor Altgeld was working to mediate the dispute between the Pullman Company and the strikers when Cleveland interfered. There should have absolutely been more time given for these sides to reach an accommodation.

It's not the job of government to regulate labor disputes, but the fact of the matter is that these strikers were allowing no rail traffic to pass through Chicago whatsoever. Something needed to be done.
Bargaining for wages is the business of a man and his employer. Collective bargaining has no place in American society, and I commend Grover Cleveland for having the courage to act decisively.
It is my dream to see a Prohibition Amendment passed before I die.
These measures are a step in the right direction. Nothing destroys so many lives in this country as does the pernicious habit of drinking alcohol.
Perhaps if our goal is to prevent drinking on Sunday, or public drunkenness, I am all for those measures. But a blanket temperance law is a different story.
Railroads gouge hardworking American farmers year after year, while giving preferred rates to large companies. I won't allow it.
I will examine this issue very carefully. If government has helped to finance some of these railroads, it's only fair for government to have a say in their operations.
Only on rare occasions where there is a clear abuse from the railroads. For the most part they simply charge what the traffic will bear.
I doubt that it is even Constitutional for the federal government to control railroad rates. This will never happen in my Administration.
It's time that the two halves of our country fully reconciled. Confederate veterans should be helped as much as Union veterans.

There's just one problem with this idea -- Confederate veterans will never accept money from the Federal government. Since they deem this idea to be an exercise in humiliation, I am left with no choice but to oppose it myself.
I will not support a program that delivers pension funds to the very men who rebelled against our Constitution. I hope this is the last time I ever have to answer this question.
One can never be sure when the inspiration of love will strike. Widows' pensions should be protected unconditionally.
Have you seen some of these couples? I believe if a marriage was initiated after 1880, then the pension benefits should cease upon the death of the veteran.

This is just another sad chapter in the fiscal mismanagement of the veterans' pensions. The best we can do now is to remain vigilant for the day when these pensions are universally offered to all aged veterans.
The entire city of Chicago and half of the Midwest was blocked to rail traffic. It was impossible for this fracas not to interrupt U.S. mail.
We should have found other methods to end this strike besides legal chicanery.
The Democrats have always been the party of states' rights. I was a little surprised to see Cleveland intervene in this case.
A good man named Eugene Debs was thrown in prison due to the overreach of President Cleveland.
There are individuals in this country working for less than a dollar a day. Only through desperation would a man ever consent to such an arrangement.
This policy is economically unviable. It is also yet another "solution" to our problems which I deem to be unconstitutional.
We accept any European who is able to read and write. America will always serve as a place where the oppressed masses can find a new hope.
We live in an open society, but that should never serve as an excuse for business to undermine the American worker by paying pauper wages to new arrivals.

It's time that we had severe restrictions on who we let into this country. A walk down the streets of New York is hardly distinguishable from the Tower of Babel, and these new arrivals crush the bargaining power of the American worker.

The international system we have in place is the gold standard. Not only is this highly advisable from a business standpoint, but it is driven by the power of Great Britain. We are better off working within this system.
This is something we should work for to reform the monetary supply. That being said, the United States should not unilaterally leave the gold standard until we have some agreement in place.

This would be a worthwhile arrangement for the laboring classes across the civilized world. When I'm elected, however, we will allow the free coinage of silver regardless of what agreements are or aren't in place.

We will vigorously enforce the Monroe Doctrine, the same way that we have since 1823. This includes support for the struggles of the people in Cuba, should they gain independence. We also appreciate Grover Cleveland's vigorous action in Venezuela last year.
I support the Monroe Doctrine as established American policy.
This is an outdated doctrine that could needlessly commit the United States to an unnecessary war. We should view any such blanket statements with grave suspicion.
This is perfectly within the realm of acceptable punishment.
I have sought the guidance of our Savior on this issue, and I cannot support the execution of our lost souls in good conscience.

The moneychangers of the temple duped (or bribed) Grover Cleveland into issuing gold bonds. While the rest of the country suffered in indignation, bankers like J.P. Morgan and the Rothschilds made off with millions.
Of course the government has a right to do this. Whether it is advisable or whether President Cleveland negotiated a good interest rate is another debate.

The federal government has every right to issue interest bearing bonds. Of course, under a solvent Administration there would be no cause for doing so. This whole episode reflects more poorly on the performance of President Cleveland than it does on any great legal issue.

description.source: What points do you wish to touch upon as you accept the Republican nomination? A written transcript will be transmitted to voters across the country.
Which of the following will be your primary campaign message?
Will you send campaigners to Nebraska, in an attempt to deliver an embarrassing defeat to Bryan, or should those resources be focused on South Dakota, Wyoming, and Iowa?
Bryan's nomination has electrified the western voter, and he is now planning to campaign on the rails, six days a week. Will you break precedent as well and make a speaking tour of the nation?
The United States is in the midst of a financial calamity, with masses of unemployed men on the streets. What will you do to revive business in this country?
You have the support of the important newspapers, and they are willing to accept your guidance on the proper campaign message. What do you want them to print?
Some of the border states (Virginia, Maryland, Kentucky) are very close this year. Do you have a strategy to make these states jump to the Republican side?
What is your definitive position on the tariff issue?
Grover Cleveland sent federal troops to Illinois to end the Pullman Strike without the request of Governor Altgeld. Was this an overreach on his part?
Can you state your definitive position on the American monetary system?
What is your opinion on measures that would aim to restrict the sale or production of alcohol?
The West Coast is a very competitive region. Can you make the case for Republican policies there, particularly in those places such as San Francisco which rely on foreign trade?
What is your interpretation of the antitrust statutes? Do large American business profit from monopolistic practices?
Do you think that local jurisdictions should be allowed to use hanging or other forms of capital punishment for crimes?

John Palmer, a Gold Democrat, is also running against Bryan. He has offered to remove his name from the ballot on the East and West Coast if you will do the same in the South. He argues that this will consolidate the anti-Bryan vote. What do you think?
Is it generally appropriate for federal courts to issue injunctions against striking unions?
Do you think that there should be federal oversight of the New York and Chicago trading markets?
Grover Cleveland led the push to repeal the Sherman Silver Purchase Act in 1894. What are your thoughts on his actions during that period?
Some labor leaders have called for regulation standardizing a ten or even an eight hour workday. Do you support these calls?
The Wilson-Gorman Tariff Act of 1894 lowered the rates on many goods, while still falling well short of Cleveland's ideal levels. What do you think about this act as a whole?
In general, is the Supreme Court too obstructionist in their rulings on economic issues? Would you appoint judges who would bring a new perspective to these issues?
Would you support a program to compensate workers who are injured on the job? Is this a proper responsibility of the federal government?
What do you have to say about William Jennings Bryan's campaign, at a high level?
Should there be greater regulation or even price controls on railroad shipping rates?
There is one week left until election day. Every state is important, but where will you give an extra push with what is left of your financial resources to educate the American voters?
I am a proud "wet" in the alcohol debate. What a man drinks is no one's business but his own.
My opponent's ideas are almost as dangerous to the survival of the United States as the Democratic traitors were in the 1860s.
I am the candidate who brings the reasonable, tested ideas of sound money, protection, and prosperity. Bryan on the other hand will usher in radicalism and instability.
My campaign will reach out to workers across the American spectrum, while Bryan's policies will leave them defenseless against foreign competition and will debase their wages.

My administration will bring back the era of the budget surplus, and will work towards the professionalization of the federal government. We will continue to phase out the 'spoils system' in accordance with the Pendleton Act.
I appreciate the faith of the American people and consult always with the Lord before I make my decisions. I will run a moderate, sensible agenda that appeals to the broad majority.
Labor agitators and agrarian radicals are threatening to overthrow our system of government. They have put forward a preposterous array of Constitutional Amendments and confiscatory welfare programs.
Democrats who believe in the gold standard are welcome in our party. We will increase tariffs, to be sure, but in a moderate way that addresses their concerns.
William Jennings Bryan makes an eloquent appeal to the heart. It's important for voters to realize that his solutions will not help our country.
Bryan's naked ambition knows no bounds. It is unbecoming of a candidate to make campaign appearances on his own behalf.

There's no way I can compete with Bryan's oratorical talents. Instead, I will receive groups of visitors at my home in Canton, Ohio. We have the financing to pay for these visits, and anyone who shows up will receive a free sandwich while I deliver a speech.
Bryan combines vague, non-sensical appeals to emotion with a near-blasphemous use of religious symbolism. I'm confident that the voters will reject this demagogue.
Free coinage of silver will debase our currency and make a mockery of us to the rest of the world.
William Jennings Bryan is a devout, honest man. It's unfortunate that he proposes such misguided policies.
Our campaign is much better positioned to address the concerns of ordinary Americans than Bryan's. He is overly focused on the silver issue.
I can't attack Bryan like the papers can without losing some of my luster. Let them publish the defamatory cartoons and opinion pieces.

The big newspapers should remind the voters that I represent a return to prosperity after the Democratic disaster of the previous four years. They should be paying as little attention to Bryan as possible.
I'm not comfortable coordinating my message with the press. I trust that they will find the right way to present a contrast between me and my opponent.
Absolutely not. Can you imagine how it would look if we removed ourselves from the ticket in any state? And for an old man like Palmer?
If Palmer will remove himself from the ballot in Kentucky, Indiana, West Virginia, Maryland, and Delaware, then I will give him free reign in the Deep South.

I hope Palmer will see fit to remove himself unilaterally from the most hotly contested border states. His is purely a protest candidacy however, and I cannot remove myself from a ballot on his behalf without looking like a buffoon.

I am willing to make an expansive deal with Palmer. He may remain on the ballot in Illinois, but must remove himself completely from the other northern states. In turn I will give him free reign in the entire South.
Bryan would drive the important railroads of this region, such as Union Pacific, into bankruptcy by reneging on agreed-upon financing arrangements.
Bryan is the type of do-gooder politician who would attempt to impose his own morality on this independent region.
One of my highest priorities in office will be a canal through Nicaragua, which will greatly enhance our national trade. Democrats lack the ambition for such far-reaching projects.
Much of California's livelihood comes from gold mining. I reject any call to undermine gold through the free coinage of silver.
There is a certain element of conservatism in the southern states. I don't think that their temperament aligns with that of Bryan. I will simply repeat the message that he is a radical.
As a Civil War veteran, I am uniquely positioned to preach a message of sectional unity and Americanism. These states must know that we have allowed bygones to be bygones.
There is a burgeoning textile industry in the Upper South. Their success depends on cheap cotton, protection, and an absence of destabilizing labor issues.
I will remind them that we support Cuban independence.
We are running a 45-state strategy. I want our victory and repudiation of the silver Democrats to be as large as possible.
That's not a good idea. Let's be realistic and devote our efforts to the states that matter.
Our speakers should converge on Illinois from all directions. We need to blanket this state with advertising and with political parades.
Let's take the fight to Bryan. I want us to be campaigning the hardest in Missouri, Nebraska, Kansas, and Iowa. Our extra cash will ensure a landslide on election night.
Let's continue to focus on the Midwest. Ohio, Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, etc.
I want us to put all of our spare resources into Iowa and Minnesota.
We need to shore up our base. Let's make sure we win in Pennsylvania and New York, where the stakes are highest.
I support a strict adherence to the gold standard, which is fundamental to American prosperity.
Limited silver coinage is a good compromise. I support a program like that of Bland-Allison where the government purchases around $2 million of silver each month.

I support the free, unlimited coinage of silver at the current market price of 30-to-1 against gold. This ratio should be frequently adjusted to match actual prices in order to avoid another run on the Treasury's gold supply.
I support the free, unlimited coinage of silver at a fixed price ratio of 16-to-1 against gold.
Tariffs should be limited to the minimum amount necessary to raise sufficient revenue for the federal government.
In limited areas where we have new industries forming, tariffs can be higher. They should be low on most products.
Where we have mature, stable industries, tariffs can be lower. They should be high on most products.
We need high tariffs on a variety of products and commodities to stimulate American manufacturing.

The Democratic idea has been that if you legislate to make the masses prosperous, their prosperity will find its way up through every class which rests upon them. We need to help our farmers and our workers by allowing the coinage of silver.
It's time we think about implementing a series of public works projects to occupy our excess labor force. This will improve business by placing more money in the hands of consumers.
I can't stress this enough. The most important thing we can do right now is increase our tariffs to protect American business.
We need to reaffirm our commitment to non-intervention in business affairs. Companies need stability before they will have the confidence to expand.
This was the act of a tyrant. Pullman was engaged in abominable business practices, and in the darkest hour Cleveland cast his lot with the company over the working man.

Governor Altgeld was working to mediate the dispute between the Pullman Company and the strikers when Cleveland interfered. There should have absolutely been more time given for these sides to reach an accommodation.

It's not the job of government to regulate labor disputes, but the fact of the matter is that these strikers were allowing no rail traffic to pass through Chicago whatsoever. Something needed to be done.
Bargaining for wages is the business of a man and his employer. Collective bargaining has no place in American society, and I commend Grover Cleveland for having the courage to act decisively.
It is my dream to see a Prohibition Amendment passed before I die.
These measures are a step in the right direction. Nothing destroys so many lives in this country as does the pernicious habit of drinking alcohol.
Perhaps if our goal is to prevent drinking on Sunday, or public drunkenness, I am all for those measures. But a blanket temperance law is a different story.
Anyone who knows me should know the answer to this question. I support the free coinage of silver at a price ratio of 16-to-1 versus gold.

I support the coinage of silver, and this action was a step in the wrong direction. It took money out of the system when we needed it the most, and is partly to blame for the depth of our current downturn.

Unfortunately the Treasury was bankrupt. I do think that Cleveland approached this in the usual heavy-handed, abrasive manner, but he was absolutely in the right. This whole episode demonstrates the folly of silver coinage.
We can criticize Cleveland for a lot of things, but his repeal of the Silver Purchase Act is not one of them. I supported Cleveland all the way in the repeal debate.
We would also like to move a little more in the direction of lower tariffs, but overall this is a good law.

I am disappointed with the half measures taken in this act. If Senators were directly elected by the people, they would be less beholden to the types of financial interests who wrote their own tariffs into this law.
This act was the result of countless hours of compromise and negotiations. It's time we closed this issue and stopped changing our entire tariff system every time a new Administration takes over.
My first action as President will be to reinstate higher tariffs. This is an American policy that supports American factories and American workers.
When I am President, you will finally have someone who takes our antitrust legislation seriously. I will break up monopolistic banks and railroads in places where they stifle competition.
I take a very narrow view of the term "monopoly". There is a need for these statutes but they open up a lot of danger for political witch hunts.
I favor a hands-off approach to the economy. The federal government has no business stepping in and breaking a company into pieces.
Railroads gouge hardworking American farmers year after year, while giving preferred rates to large companies. I won't allow it.
I will examine this issue very carefully. If government has helped to finance some of these railroads, it's only fair for government to have a say in their operations.
Only on rare occasions where there is a clear abuse from the railroads. For the most part they simply charge what the traffic will bear.
I doubt that it is even Constitutional for the federal government to control railroad rates. This will never happen in my Administration.
We absolutely need a federal program for this purpose. The Bible says that we must love all people -- even those who have been cast aside by our Darwinian industrial machinery.
This is more properly a state responsibility. It is outside the scope of the federal government to regulate working conditions in this manner.
It is the responsibility of the worker to put aside such funds as are necessary to protect them from these events. This is why we have mutual aid societies in place.
Not only would this greatly improve working conditions for Americans, it would increase employment by spreading our working hours amongst more people.
I am a strong supporter of labor, but I also think that working hour restrictions are more appropriate for women and children than for grown men.
I do not see the authority for regulating this under the Commerce Clause of the Constitution. This is something that individual states would need to investigate.
I don't believe that outside parties should regulate the working arrangements between a man and his employer.
If we could manage it, I would increase the number of justices on the Court so that we can dissipate the influence of the reactionaries presently in control there.
Absolutely. I will appoint sensible, assertive judges as President. The purpose of the Court is not to simply overturn half of the laws passed by Congress, on picayune Constitutional objections.
It is not my place as a politician, running for a position in the Executive Branch, to comment on the performance of the Court.

The poor man is called a socialist if he believes that the wealth of the rich should be divided among the poor, but the rich man is called a financier if he devises a plan by which the pittance of the poor can be converted to his use.
It was stock market and railroad company chicanery which caused the Panic of 1893. Sensible regulation of this process could have saved us all a lot of trouble.
The New York Stock Exchange is a private company providing liquidity to other companies. The last thing our fragile economy needs is some hare-brained intervention in this process.
There has already been considerable reform of the stock markets since the dangerous days of the 1860s. There's no need to take this idea any further.
This is perfectly within the realm of acceptable punishment.
I have sought the guidance of our Savior on this issue, and I cannot support the execution of our lost souls in good conscience.
The use of injunctions is a favored court tactic for union busting and it must stop. I support the right of striking workers to picket their workplace while on strike.

Maybe in limited cases, where unions are a threat to public safety or where they undermine an essential industry. The courts are notoriously conservative, however, and definitely take this practice too far.

The Pullman Strike of 1894 disrupted half of the nation's rail traffic and threatened to throw our society into complete turmoil. A small group of radicals should never have the power to disrupt the lives of millions.

description.source: Which of the following most closely matches your overall campaign message?

You have alluded to the need for less prejudice between the races. Senator "Pitchfork" Ben Tillman, of South Carolina, privately seeks your clarification.
Can you reassure him that the federal government will respect the rights of the states under your Administration?

Perhaps the media attention would be beneficial in building excitement for your campaign on a national scale?
Can you state your definitive position on the American monetary system?

What do you have to say about William McKinley's campaign, at a high level?

The novelty of a personal visit from the "Great Commoner" could probably swing the West Coast states in your direction. However, it will take two weeks to travel and return via train.

What is your definitive position on the tariff issue?
What is your opinion on measures that would aim to restrict the sale or production of alcohol?

Do you think that there should be federal oversight of the New York and Chicago trading markets?
Do you believe that immigrant labor is undermining the American worker? Should there be some restrictions put into place on immigration?
Can you respond to rumors that you would seek to abolish the Supreme Court if elected, due to their recent decisions on the income tax and antitrust issues?
Is it generally appropriate for federal courts to issue injunctions against striking unions?
Critics have said that you wrap yourself in religious imagery too much for a presidential candidate. What is your response?
Do you support greater regulation on the sale and labeling of opium, cocaine, and morphine when used in patent medicines?
Should corporations be permitted to hire private detectives for security, and to infiltrate into labor movements?
You are making a big speech in Chicago today. What points will you touch on?
The federal deficit has recently increased after two decades of steady decline. What are your thoughts on this?

What is your opinion on the overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy by the Dole group? Do you support the annexation of Hawaii into the United States?
A few western states have allowed women the right to vote. Do you take the calls for a women's suffrage Amendment seriously?
Are you prepared to reaffirm our commitment to the Monroe Doctrine, should any new territories in Latin America gain independence from Spain?
There is one week left until election day. Every state is important, but where will you give an extra push with your personal campaigning to swing the final results?
I am a proud "wet" in the alcohol debate. What a man drinks is no one's business but his own.
We support the free coinage of silver priced at a 16-to-1 ratio against gold. The results will aid farmers and workers of all classes and contribute to an American renewal.

We will focus on free-silver and especially on the issues affecting farmers. We will seek a reduction in private debts and an end to the monopolistic practices of the railroads. We will also fight for the lowest possible tariffs.
Silver coinage is just one part of my platform. Let's not forget the struggles of the urban worker in his efforts to unionize and obtain fair wages.
I am 100% committed to the coinage of silver. It's important however, that we strike a moderate tone on other issues to expand our appeal as widely as we can.
McKinley is a fanatical defender of an obsolete monetary system. He is a front-man for big business and the New York financiers.
McKinley's support of high tariffs is a crime which strangles American commerce. Similar protectionist programs have twice been rejected by American voters in the past ten years alone.
We may have our disagreements, but William McKinley is an honorable man. Our campaign will focus on the issues, not on the opponent.
McKinley's insistence on the gold standard has alienated many prominent Republicans from his own party, such as Henry Teller.
The Supreme Court has consistently stood in the way of progress by implementing an overly narrow interpretation of the Constitution. I support drastic measures to reduce its influence.
There have been some terrible decisions made by the Court. We might consider some measures to make the court more accountable to the popular will.
This is an unfounded rumor that the McKinley campaign has disseminated to discredit my candidacy.
8 years of a William Jennings Bryan presidency will leave the Court in much better shape to address our nation's problems.
Let us bring our message to the citizens of the Pacific Coast. Winning these three states could swing the entire election.
Let's keep the tour as short as possible. I will take a train to San Francisco and deliver a few speeches in that city, but will not tour the entire coast.
There is no time for that diversion. Heaven knows what rumors McKinley will spread while I am gone, and winning the Midwest should be our primary focus.
New York is a traditional Democratic stronghold, and I'm confident that the people of that state will support my message. We will campaign there extensively.
Let's not waste our time in a hostile state. We must sow our seed upon the good earth where it will multiply.
I will give one big speech in New York City to open my campaign. Even if winning that state is hopeless, we need the national press.
The humblest citizen in all the land, when clad in the armor of a righteous cause, is stronger than all the hosts of error.
The word of the Lord demands that we give our attention to the poor, the sick, and the feeble. This campaign is not about me -- I am a mere servant of Christ.
I'm not sure what kind of Christianity the Republicans adhere to, but it is of dubious merit in guiding our government.
We will respect the rights of the states. I call for greater understanding, but certainly not for an overthrow of the natural order.
There has been a deafening silence for many years on the issue of equal rights in the South. It's time we had a true enforcement of the 14th and 15th Amendment.

Tillman and others have nothing to fear from me. It is the sacred duty of the white man to properly instruct and civilize the black man and other inferior races. Greater understanding must occur within this context.
We need to keep it simple. Our primary goal in this campaign is to win the critical states of Iowa, Illinois, and Indiana.
It's a shame that we need to even campaign in these beacons of the South. But if we have to, let us do it with effluence.
I will make my standard stump speech highlighting the dangers of the gold standard and advocating for free silver.
Let's hit on the issue of tariffs. These voters need to be reminded that tariffs increase the cost of farm equipment and other manufactured goods.
I will speak to the general issues of the future -- free silver, higher wages, worker's rights, an end to child labor, and women's suffrage.
I am a moderate who supports the free coinage of silver. I am not a radical as so many claim. It is McKinley's antiquated insistence on the gold standard that is truly radical.
I support a strict adherence to the gold standard, which is fundamental to American prosperity.
Limited silver coinage is a good compromise. I support a program like that of Bland-Allison where the government purchases around $2 million of silver each month.

I support the free, unlimited coinage of silver at the current market price of 30-to-1 against gold. This ratio should be frequently adjusted to match actual prices in order to avoid another run on the Treasury's gold supply.
I support the free, unlimited coinage of silver at a fixed price ratio of 16-to-1 against gold.
Tariffs should be limited to the minimum amount necessary to raise sufficient revenue for the federal government.
In limited areas where we have new industries forming, tariffs can be higher. They should be low on most products.
Where we have mature, stable industries, tariffs can be lower. They should be high on most products.
We need high tariffs on a variety of products and commodities to stimulate American manufacturing.

The Democratic idea has been that if you legislate to make the masses prosperous, their prosperity will find its way up through every class which rests upon them. We need to help our farmers and our workers by allowing the coinage of silver.
It's time we think about implementing a series of public works projects to occupy our excess labor force. This will improve business by placing more money in the hands of consumers.
I can't stress this enough. The most important thing we can do right now is increase our tariffs to protect American business.
We need to reaffirm our commitment to non-intervention in business affairs. Companies need stability before they will have the confidence to expand.
This was the act of a tyrant. Pullman was engaged in abominable business practices, and in the darkest hour Cleveland cast his lot with the company over the working man.

It's not the job of government to regulate labor disputes, but the fact of the matter is that these strikers were allowing no rail traffic to pass through Chicago whatsoever. Something needed to be done.
Bargaining for wages is the business of a man and his employer. Collective bargaining has no place in American society, and I commend Grover Cleveland for having the courage to act decisively.
It is my dream to see a Prohibition Amendment passed before I die.
These measures are a step in the right direction. Nothing destroys so many lives in this country as does the pernicious habit of drinking alcohol.
Perhaps if our goal is to prevent drinking on Sunday, or public drunkenness, I am all for those measures. But a blanket temperance law is a different story.
Overall the deficit is still low. Furthermore, if we allow the free coinage of silver the amount of our deficit will decrease commensurably as our currency inflates.
There would be no increase in the deficit if the Supreme Court hadn't overturned the income tax.
Once we reinstitute our tariffs, this deficit will disappear. Best of all, the lion's share of these taxes will be paid by foreign merchants.
I would support such an Amendment if it gained traction within our system. I'm just sorry to see that the chances seem unlikely.
We welcome the support of women and men. Where women are granted the vote, we are confident that they will support our ticket.
I think there are more important issues for us to be focusing our efforts on. Extending the suffrage to women carries with it a whole host of dangers.
We accept any European who is able to read and write. America will always serve as a place where the oppressed masses can find a new hope.
We live in an open society, but that should never serve as an excuse for business to undermine the American worker by paying pauper wages to new arrivals.

It's time that we had severe restrictions on who we let into this country. A walk down the streets of New York is hardly distinguishable from the Tower of Babel, and these new arrivals crush the bargaining power of the American worker.

These men are Americans and they are attempting to bring badly-needed order to the islands of Hawaii. If managed properly, an annexation will allow us to enjoy the benefits of Hawaii's innumerable sugar plantations. These islands are also a perfect location for a naval base.
This cabal may be hoping for recognition from the United States, but for now they are simply a group of Pacific island adventurers. I have no wishes for either their success or their failure.
We will never recognize or annex the so-called Hawaiian government while I am President.

The poor man is called a socialist if he believes that the wealth of the rich should be divided among the poor, but the rich man is called a financier if he devises a plan by which the pittance of the poor can be converted to his use.
It was stock market and railroad company chicanery which caused the Panic of 1893. Sensible regulation of this process could have saved us all a lot of trouble.
The New York Stock Exchange is a private company providing liquidity to other companies. The last thing our fragile economy needs is some hare-brained intervention in this process.
There has already been considerable reform of the stock markets since the dangerous days of the 1860s. There's no need to take this idea any further.

We will vigorously enforce the Monroe Doctrine, the same way that we have since 1823. This includes support for the struggles of the people in Cuba, should they gain independence. We also appreciate Grover Cleveland's vigorous action in Venezuela last year.
I support the Monroe Doctrine as established American policy.
This is an outdated doctrine that could needlessly commit the United States to an unnecessary war. We should view any such blanket statements with grave suspicion.
This is another sad attempt to crush the spirit of the working man. It's difficult to distinguish between Pinkertons and vigilantes during some of these repression actions.
Perhaps if collective bargaining was protected, companies would have less cause to fear their own employees.
I don't see who has the authority to stop this. This is another example of regulation that would fall outside of the scope of the Commerce Clause in the Constitution.
The practice of hiring detectives from agencies like the Pinkertons is justified by the militancy and danger of the American labor movement.
This is perfectly within the realm of acceptable punishment.
I have sought the guidance of our Savior on this issue, and I cannot support the execution of our lost souls in good conscience.

I'm scared to take my own medicine sometimes for fear of what might be in there. Medicines should be clearly labeled with their ingredients, so that those who wish to avoid intoxicating substances can do so.
Many patent medicine purveyors operate in a single locale, and do not cross state lines. Where appropriate, I would support regulation, but only where the Constitution allows it.
This isn't an issue we should be concerned about. Additional regulation of drugs and medicinal practice would undermine our national liberty.
The use of injunctions is a favored court tactic for union busting and it must stop. I support the right of striking workers to picket their workplace while on strike.

Maybe in limited cases, where unions are a threat to public safety or where they undermine an essential industry. The courts are notoriously conservative, however, and definitely take this practice too far.

The Pullman Strike of 1894 disrupted half of the nation's rail traffic and threatened to throw our society into complete turmoil. A small group of radicals should never have the power to disrupt the lives of millions.
Let's spend the entire week in Illinois. That is the largest state that we have a chance to win.
Let's make one last general tour of the Midwest. Starting in Ohio, we will travel west and end in North Dakota, before moving down to Nebraska on Election Day.
Let's focus on Iowa and the Dakotas. My presence can swing those states.
Indiana has always been the critical swing state. Let's spend most of our time there while also crossing over into Illinois and Kentucky.
We must secure the upper South. This means we start in in Maryland and Delaware, move through Virginia and West Virginia, and then through Kentucky.

description.source: Which of the following most closely matches your overall campaign message?
What is your definitive position on the tariff issue?
What do you have to say about William McKinley's campaign, at a high level?
What do you think of leaving the Midwest for a week and making a circuit of the crucial upper South states? (i.e. Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, West Virginia, and Kentucky)

You have very little chance of winning New York this fall, and nearly all of that city's newspapers are anti-Bryan. That doesn't mean you couldn't draw a frenzied crowd in New York City.
Perhaps the media attention would be beneficial in building excitement for your campaign on a national scale?
Grover Cleveland sent federal troops to Illinois to end the Pullman Strike without the request of Governor Altgeld. Was this an overreach on his part?
What is your opinion on measures that would aim to restrict the sale or production of alcohol?

You have alluded to the need for less prejudice between the races. Senator "Pitchfork" Ben Tillman, of South Carolina, privately seeks your clarification.
Can you reassure him that the federal government will respect the rights of the states under your Administration?
The United States is in the midst of a financial calamity, with masses of unemployed men on the streets. What will you do to revive business in this country?
Can you state your definitive position on the American monetary system?

The novelty of a personal visit from the "Great Commoner" could probably swing the West Coast states in your direction. However, it will take two weeks to travel and return via train.
Will you divert your attention from the Midwest long enough to visit California, Oregon, and Washington?
Do you approve of Grover Cleveland's handing of the federal budget over the previous four years?
Some people have suggested implementing a minimum wage, under which people may not be employed. Do you think this would help increase wages or would it simply put more men out of work?
Should the federal government make an effort to build a canal through Nicaragua to more efficiently link trade in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans?
Would you support federal "Blue Laws" to protect the sanctity of Sunday?
Will you work towards international agreements to create a monetary system based on "bimetallism", i.e. a combination of gold and silver?
What do you say to the notion that high tariffs hurt farmers?
What are your thoughts on the Women's Christian Temperance Union? Is this group a positive force in American life?

Horace Boies, the former Governor of Iowa, will be making a big speech tomorrow to capitalize on the crowds at the State Fair. Will you make the overnight trip to Iowa in time to deliver a concluding address to the farmers there?
Does the success of the tin-plate industry within the U.S. prove that protectionism stimulates industry?
Do you have any comments to make about the candidacy of John Palmer, a Gold Democrat and splinter candidate who is currently campaigning?
Are you pleased with the recent defeat in Congress of the Pacific Railroad Funding Bill, which would have provided federal support to the Southern and Central Pacific railroads.
Do you think that the United States Navy is large enough to adequately defend American interests on a global level?
Would you support an Amendment to the Constitution allowing the people to vote for their Senators directly?
There is one week left until election day. Every state is important, but where will you give an extra push with your personal campaigning to swing the final results?
I am a proud "wet" in the alcohol debate. What a man drinks is no one's business but his own.
We support the free coinage of silver priced at a 16-to-1 ratio against gold. The results will aid farmers and workers of all classes and contribute to an American renewal.

We will focus on free-silver and especially on the issues affecting farmers. We will seek a reduction in private debts and an end to the monopolistic practices of the railroads. We will also fight for the lowest possible tariffs.
Silver coinage is just one part of my platform. Let's not forget the struggles of the urban worker in his efforts to unionize and obtain fair wages.
I am 100% committed to the coinage of silver. It's important however, that we strike a moderate tone on other issues to expand our appeal as widely as we can.
McKinley is a fanatical defender of an obsolete monetary system. He is a front-man for big business and the New York financiers.
McKinley's support of high tariffs is a crime which strangles American commerce. Similar protectionist programs have twice been rejected by American voters in the past ten years alone.
We may have our disagreements, but William McKinley is an honorable man. Our campaign will focus on the issues, not on the opponent.
McKinley's insistence on the gold standard has alienated many prominent Republicans from his own party, such as Henry Teller.
Let us bring our message to the citizens of the Pacific Coast. Winning these three states could swing the entire election.
Let's keep the tour as short as possible. I will take a train to San Francisco and deliver a few speeches in that city, but will not tour the entire coast.
There is no time for that diversion. Heaven knows what rumors McKinley will spread while I am gone, and winning the Midwest should be our primary focus.
New York is a traditional Democratic stronghold, and I'm confident that the people of that state will support my message. We will campaign there extensively.
Let's not waste our time in a hostile state. We must sow our seed upon the good earth where it will multiply.
I will give one big speech in New York City to open my campaign. Even if winning that state is hopeless, we need the national press.
We will respect the rights of the states. I call for greater understanding, but certainly not for an overthrow of the natural order.
There has been a deafening silence for many years on the issue of equal rights in the South. It's time we had a true enforcement of the 14th and 15th Amendment.

Tillman and others have nothing to fear from me. It is the sacred duty of the white man to properly instruct and civilize the black man and other inferior races. Greater understanding must occur within this context.
We need to focus more on Indiana and Michigan. Iowa should already be in the bag for us.
Boies's time has passed. We need to avoid appearing with such radical politicians and cultivate the moderate wing of the party.
Absolutely. I would be honored to give this speech.
We need to keep it simple. Our primary goal in this campaign is to win the critical states of Iowa, Illinois, and Indiana.
It's a shame that we need to even campaign in these beacons of the South. But if we have to, let us do it with effluence.
It's a shame that Grover Cleveland allowed his supporters to bolt the party the moment it became clear their faction had lost this year's nomination.
Good riddance. On the issue of silver coinage, you are either with us or you're with the industrialists. Palmer has shown his cards.
I don't know how this man could live with four years of William McKinley just to save the face of his friend Grover Cleveland. No true Democrat would vote for him.
I'm very concerned about John Palmer. If he is gaining support maybe it means there is a valid criticism we must face up to.
I support a strict adherence to the gold standard, which is fundamental to American prosperity.
Limited silver coinage is a good compromise. I support a program like that of Bland-Allison where the government purchases around $2 million of silver each month.

I support the free, unlimited coinage of silver at the current market price of 30-to-1 against gold. This ratio should be frequently adjusted to match actual prices in order to avoid another run on the Treasury's gold supply.
I support the free, unlimited coinage of silver at a fixed price ratio of 16-to-1 against gold.
Tariffs should be limited to the minimum amount necessary to raise sufficient revenue for the federal government.
In limited areas where we have new industries forming, tariffs can be higher. They should be low on most products.
Where we have mature, stable industries, tariffs can be lower. They should be high on most products.
We need high tariffs on a variety of products and commodities to stimulate American manufacturing.

The Democratic idea has been that if you legislate to make the masses prosperous, their prosperity will find its way up through every class which rests upon them. We need to help our farmers and our workers by allowing the coinage of silver.
It's time we think about implementing a series of public works projects to occupy our excess labor force. This will improve business by placing more money in the hands of consumers.
I can't stress this enough. The most important thing we can do right now is increase our tariffs to protect American business.
We need to reaffirm our commitment to non-intervention in business affairs. Companies need stability before they will have the confidence to expand.
This was the act of a tyrant. Pullman was engaged in abominable business practices, and in the darkest hour Cleveland cast his lot with the company over the working man.

Governor Altgeld was working to mediate the dispute between the Pullman Company and the strikers when Cleveland interfered. There should have absolutely been more time given for these sides to reach an accommodation.

It's not the job of government to regulate labor disputes, but the fact of the matter is that these strikers were allowing no rail traffic to pass through Chicago whatsoever. Something needed to be done.
Bargaining for wages is the business of a man and his employer. Collective bargaining has no place in American society, and I commend Grover Cleveland for having the courage to act decisively.
It is my dream to see a Prohibition Amendment passed before I die.
These measures are a step in the right direction. Nothing destroys so many lives in this country as does the pernicious habit of drinking alcohol.
Perhaps if our goal is to prevent drinking on Sunday, or public drunkenness, I am all for those measures. But a blanket temperance law is a different story.
This is the type of cronyism that occurs when government selects certain industries for protection under a tariff act. I support low tariffs across the board.
I'm glad for the men who produce tin for a living, but we need to consider the overall effect of this policy. I don't have a glib answer for you at this point.
There is nothing I'm more proud of from my time in Congress than creating the conditions that allowed for a booming tin industry to flourish within our borders.
The answer here is obvious. High tariffs force farmers to purchase overpriced equipment and do nothing to increase crop prices.
Perhaps. It depends on if these tariffs cause other countries to retaliate against our agricultural goods. This is always a risk when tariffs are increased in haphazard fashion.
High tariffs protect American industry and increase the purchasing power of the consumer. Free silver would throw this system into chaos and even hurt the farmer in the long-term.
The current system for selecting Senators is unimaginably corrupt. State legislatures have every incentive to select the most corrupt, retrograde candidate for the job.
I neither support, nor do I oppose this idea for an Amendment. My job as President will be to enforce the law as it stands.
The purpose of the Senate is to act as an objective legislative body. It is dangerous to tamper with the Constitutional provisions established by our founding fathers.
The WCTU is one of the most spiritually uplifting, morally righteous groups in our society. I pray that the Lord will see fit to guide them to success in their mission.
This is a well-meaning group of honest Christian women. I am neither especially opposed to nor especially supportive of their goals.
This group is Exhibit A in the dangers of allowing women to become politically active. They are engaged in a naive quest to purify American life from an imagined evil.
There are individuals in this country working for less than a dollar a day. Only through desperation would a man ever consent to such an arrangement.
This policy is economically unviable. It is also yet another "solution" to our problems which I deem to be unconstitutional.
At the very least, a federal law prohibiting the sale of alcohol of Sunday seems appropriate.
This debate has no place in our system of federalism. The individual states have every right to decide how they wish to handle the issue of commerce and drinking on Sunday.
I don't support the mandated closing of shops on Sunday.

The international system we have in place is the gold standard. Not only is this highly advisable from a business standpoint, but it is driven by the power of Great Britain. We are better off working within this system.
This is something we should work for to reform the monetary supply. That being said, the United States should not unilaterally leave the gold standard until we have some agreement in place.

This would be a worthwhile arrangement for the laboring classes across the civilized world. When I'm elected, however, we will allow the free coinage of silver regardless of what agreements are or aren't in place.
The Navy is more than adequate to meet our current needs, and will remain so as long as imperialist Republicans avoid intervening in Cuba or Hawaii.
I am disappointed with the backward status of our Navy. We need a more vigorous fleet, and we need a canal in Nicaragua to more closely link our two coasts.

Grover Cleveland has vetoed more pieces of legislation than any President in our history, increased our deficit, and still found a way to provide J.P. Morgan with a financial windfall from the public purse.
Is there anyone left in the United States who approves of Grover Cleveland? We need to move on from his failed Administration.
Grover Cleveland is a citizen of integrity who has done his best under trying circumstances. He was simply found to be not up to the job.
I will stand up for Grover Cleveland for the rest of my life. I believe that he is a great man whom our history will greatly vindicate.
It is my firm position that we need to nationalize the railroads of this country. Their power has stood beyond reproach for too long.

For all of their talk about small government, the Republicans are quite adept at funneling public money to the railroads. I only support that practice when there is a clear rationale, and in this case the rationale was corruption.
Without federal support including loans and land grants, there are certain railroads which would simply be too large to construct with private capital. I was disappointed by the defeat of this bill.
I was opposed to this bill. We might have provided land grants and funding for railroads in the past, but that practice will end under my Administration.
I envision an American canal, built by American workers, property of the American government, supporting the actions of a robust American Navy. I fully support these plans.
This could be a fantastic method of creating work for our idle workers. What better way is there to implement a massive public works project?
Am I understand that we will be sending thousands of men to dig through the hills of Nicaragua on this pipe dream of a project? Allow me to predict that there will never be a canal in that country.
Let's spend the entire week in Illinois. That is the largest state that we have a chance to win.
Let's make one last general tour of the Midwest. Starting in Ohio, we will travel west and end in North Dakota, before moving down to Nebraska on Election Day.
Let's focus on Iowa and the Dakotas. My presence can swing those states.
Indiana has always been the critical swing state. Let's spend most of our time there while also crossing over into Illinois and Kentucky.
We must secure the upper South. This means we start in in Maryland and Delaware, move through Virginia and West Virginia, and then through Kentucky.

description.source: Martin Van Buren, Democrat and President until 1841, will be making a tour of the country to visit various friends and political figures. Will you extend the invitation for him to stay at your estate for a few days?
What points will emphasize in your acceptance letter, as you accept the Whig nomination for President?
What position will you take on the Texas annexation issue?
What should your party's position be on the Tariff of 1842, which increased tariffs?
Do you support an Amendment that would limit the President to a single term in office?
Do you believe that some revenue should be set aside from our tariffs to finance internal improvements, such as canals and roads?
What is your current position on the banking system?
There are a number of attacks which focus on your fondness for horse-racing, drinking, gambling, female conversation, and the like. Do you have a response to this?
Does it make sense to attack Northern Democrats as enablers and fellow travelers of the Southern slavery expansion?
There have recently been riots and armed clashes between nativists and Irish immigrants in Philadelphia and elsewhere. Do you have any plans to condemn the Irish violence in these episodes?
Cassius Clay, your cousin, has published a letter stating you are in accord with the abolitionist movement. How will you respond to this?
Is there something you can do to give the Southern Whigs political cover from the incessant attacks that they are in league with an anti-slavery party?
Do you plan to make any attacks against the Liberty Party, a radical abolitionist group that is fielding a third party candidate?
Do you still support the idea that the federal government should purchase the telegraph patent and manage the technology?
Was there really a bargain (a “Corrupt Bargain” to many) between yourself and John Quincy Adams which elevated him to the Presidency in 1825?
Aside from the issue of Texas, do you support the expansion of the United States in general? Into Oregon, other parts of Mexico, Cuba, etc.?
Do you support any effort to establish a unified, national currency?
Do you agree with Robert Walker's letter, arguing that that slavery issue will be diluted by national expansion?
Regardless of your personal feelings, would you sign an act which established an independent Treasury for the government's funds?
Do you support any changes to our current naturalization laws?
Do you have any criticism of the authorities in Illinois, regarding their failure to properly protect Joseph Smith before his assassination in June?
Do you support the lifting of the Gag Rule in Congress?
What is your position on the Oregon boundary question?
Would you sign a law that lowered tariffs below the level needed to protect American industry from foreign imports?
Is there a particular state where your party should concentrate its resources and most talented speakers as the election draws near?
Only a very limited amount, for the most compelling projects. Otherwise the tariff should be for revenue purposes only.
It might be best if I don't appear overly friendly to leading Democrats. Especially one as unpopular as Van Buren.
This would be a strictly personal invite. We are friends. And besides, it might blunt some opposition to my candidacy from New York.
I stand opposed to any annexation of Texas. It will reopen settled questions and distract our nation from its important political issues, such as economic development.

I support the annexation of Texas, so long as the admission of that state is paired with the admission of a free state. I will briefly mention that my positions on other issues are well-known and remain the same.
I will avoid any mention of Texas. The main focus of my acceptance will be an elucidation of my economic principles, including a national bank, a tariff, and internal improvemnets.
I will strike a middle ground on the Texas question, supporting annexation so long as it doesn't lead to war with Mexico, or to significant opposition from any section of the country.
This discussion has grown tiresome, but let me restate that I support the annexation of Texas.
This discussion has grown tiresome, but I will continue to advocate for a moderate solution on this issue.
This discussion has grown tiresome, but let me restate that I oppose the annexation of Texas.
We should condemn the apparent lawlessness of the Irish arrivals, and ask whether we ought to reconsider our generous naturalization policies.
It's best if we avoid making any statements on this issue.
After a few days have passed and tempers have cooled, let us reemphasize our support for current naturalization laws.
We must put out a letter, clarifying that we only support abolition if slaveholders can be fairly compensated, with reasonable notice, and if freed slaves can be recolonized to Africa.
We must attack Cassius Clay's statements at once, for the dishonest falsehoods that they are. I am in no way an abolitionist in this debate.
I'm not going to dignify this letter with a response.
There are a lot of places in America where men like that kind of thing. We will win the Yankee Puritan vote in any case.
I've undertaken the amusements of our times, perhaps a little more than most, but it has never had any bearing on the work I have done.
In anticipation of this attack, I've actually made some effort in the past year or so to scale back my amusements. I don't believe it is ever too late for a man to change their conduct.
Any attacks we make will only publicize this group more. Let's stick to our own campaign in this case.
Thomas Birney is a stooge of the Democrats, attempting to agitate emotions and divide our party. People ought to feel free to vote for him if they want to hand this election to James K. Polk.
I am steadfast against the annexation of Texas and the expansion of slavery. I believe that Birney's followers should be made aware of this point.
I absolutely believe that the development of telegraph lines should take its place alongside canals, harbors, and railroads as a national prerogative.
I've supported internal improvements throughout my career, but telegraph lines are a different thing. I trust that private individuals can build these.
Let's not make any divisive statements on this issue. The public is hardly clamoring for my opinion in any case.
I don't know how many times a man can deny an unjust allegation before fatigue sets in.
My opposition to the annexation of Texas is known, but we could more explicitly tie that maneuver to the expansion of slavery.
We should attack the Northern Democrats on their opposition to, or flip-flopping on, the issues of tariffs and internal improvements. They are on soft ground in that debate.
I am as much in favor of the annexation of Texas as Mr. Polk is. To insinuate otherwise is nothing but dishonesty writ large.
I am opposed to radicalism from any region, and that includes anti-slavery radicalism. The Whig Party is a national party with a national program that will benefit all regions equally.
We stand steadfast in support of this tariff. It is one of the few positive accomplishments of Mr. Tyler's so-called Presidency.
The primary purpose of our tariffs should be revenue. But should a small amount of protection incidentally occur from our tariff policy, that is acceptable.
We should avoid taking a strong position on this tariff. There are men in our party who stand on both sides of the issue.
We must rescind this tariff and replace it with something much lower. I support free trade and low tariffs.
This is one of the key objectives of our current tariff policy, and I would support a strong infrastructure program as President.
I don't believe that it is constitutional or advisable for the federal government to undertake an internal improvements program.
I stand for a national bank, broadly similar to the late Second Bank of the United States.
I stand for a national bank or an independent Treasury -- whichever can gain the most support. I would require any national bank to maintain a branch in every state.
I will never support a national bank, but I do advocate an independent Treasury, so that federal funds won't be tied up in local speculations.
I support our current free banking system, and I see no need for the Treasury to insulate its operations from the state-chartered banks.
This is a necessary step against the overreach and abuse of power of the Executive branch.
I don't support an Amendment on this issue, but I will personally promise not to run for reelection.
I don't think that this is a necessary step, at this time.
Congress must function in an orderly fashion, without taking time out from its business to receive ill-conceived petitions. I support the Gag Rule.
Regardless of our feelings about the slavery issue, it is undemocratic for Congress to deny the people the right to petition the government. I believe the Gag Rule should be lifted.
We have no plans to address the Gag Rule during our campaign.
I am against the annexation of Texas. And just to show that this does derive from sectional prejudice, I am also against expansion into Oregon or other regions.
I believe that the United States, in line with the “Manifest Destiny” ideal, should expand wherever feasible.
I would be forced to veto such a measure as President.
Regardless of my personal feelings, it is not the place of the President to override the will of Congress, unless the law in question is unconstitutional.
I would gladly sign such a bill into law.
I support our current naturalization laws as they stand.
Only some very minor changes, like increasing the waiting period before new citizens may vote.
Our current laws are in need of great revision, in light of the troubles we have had with recent immigrants.
I support a national bank, and one clear argument for the bank is the total chaos we've had with our currency since 1837.
Only if we could establish one without chartering a new national bank.
I support an independent Treasury, but not one that would disseminate a national currency.
Our current system is more democratic than any alternative that could be devised. Let the private banks issue currency in line with their own strength and prosperity.
I believe this letter to be disingenuous at best. Further expansion will reopen the debate on slavery rather than suppress it.
We won't address Mr. Walker's letter directly, but we are in favor of annexation.
The independent Treasury is a halfway measure, designed to cover for the disaster that was the war against the Second Bank of the United States.
I would prefer a national bank, but I would be willing to sign a bill which created an independent Treasury.
The creation of an independent Treasury will be one of the key initiatives of my Presidency.
I support our current banking system, and would not support any ill-conceived attempts to centralize our finances.
We need to be just as aggressive on this issue as we are anywhere else. “Fifty-four Forty or Fight!”
We need to negotiate a permanent agreement with Great Britain that grants some of all of the Oregon Territory to the United States.
I would support any agreement, as long as the United States keeps the land that is south and east of the Colombia River.
Regardless of our personal feelings, it always concerning when a religious leader and Presidential candidate can simply be killed by a mob.
This is not an issue that we plan to address in our campaign.

Pennsylvania

Oregon is a different issue than that of Texas. In Oregon we have an existing, legitimate claim.
Virginia
